steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction and related work for a theory paper that proves linear mode connectivity (up to permutation) of neural networks using optimal transport, with a formal definition of the problem and an outline of our results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Loss landscape of DNNs; connecting two local minima; applications
- Mode connectivity phenomenon
- Formal definitions: error barrier, mode connectivity, LMC
- Permutation invariance and LMC modulo permutation
- Related work: OT alignment, weight matching, dropout stability, initialization results
- Our aim and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Training DNNs: high-dimensional, non-convex optimization
  - SGD and derivatives find local minimum with low test error; landscape still has open questions
  - prior work: connect two minima from independent runs (different initialization, data orders)
  - applications: model averaging, loss landscape study, adversarial robustness, generalization theory
- Mode connectivity
  - continuous low-loss path connecting all local minima of an optimization procedure
  - extensively studied; non-linear paths for DNNs on MNIST and CIFAR10
- Formal setup
  - networks A, B with common architecture \hat{f}, parameters \theta_{A}, \theta_{B}, trained on distribution P with loss \mathcal{L}
  - continuous path p from \theta_{A} to \theta_{B}
  - error barrier height: sup over t of loss along path minus linear interpolation of endpoint losses
  - mode connected: zero barrier path; LMC: linear path
- Permutation invariance
  - permuting hidden units preserves function (Figure 1, two-layer network)
  - LMC modulo permutation: permute neurons of each hidden layer of B; linear path has low loss
- Related work
  - OT soft alignment ("good match") of neurons; fusion in federated learning with local-steps
  - align B on A, then linear path; zero-loss barrier for Resnets with SGD on CIFAR10; wider better, big depth detrimental
  - dropout stable networks exhibit mode connectivity
  - mean field: wide two-layer nets with SGD dropout stable -> (non-linear) mode connectivity
  - two-layer nets LMC up to permutation at initialization (uniform independent, scaled); maybe extends to NTK regime
- This paper
  - theoretical foundations of LMC up to permutation; MLPs beyond two-layer
  - new efficient way to find permutation
  - Sec 3: two-layer mean field; LMC up to permutation; upper bound on minimal width
  - Sec 4: OT theory; tight asymptotics on minimal MLP width
  - Sec 5: sub-Gaussian parameters; deep networks; better bounds; dimension dependence; low dimensional weights as proxy of sparse feature learning; task complexity; dropout stability
  - Sec 6: validation on MNIST with SGD; implicit dimension vs. LMC; new weight matching method

steps.text:
Training deep neural networks on complex tasks is a high-dimensional, non-convex optimization problem. Stochastic gradient-based methods (i.e., SGD and its derivatives) have proven very efficient at finding a local minimum with low test error, but there are still many open questions about the loss landscape of deep neural networks (DNNs).   - continuous path p with p(0)=\theta_{A}, p(1)=\theta_{B}

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Training deep neural networks on complex tasks is a high-dimensional, non-convex optimization problem. Stochastic gradient-based methods (i.e., SGD and its derivatives) have proven very efficient at finding a local minimum with low test error, but there are still many open questions about the loss landscape of deep neural networks (DNNs). In particular, prior work tries to find ways to connect two local minima reached by two independent runs of the same stochastic algorithm with different initialization and data orders. This problem has applications in many domains like model averaging, loss landscape study, adversarial robustness or generalization theory.

The mode connectivity phenomenon is an answer to this question. It suggests that there exists a continuous low-loss path that connects all the local minima found by a given optimization procedure. Mode connectivity has been studied extensively in the literature, and non-linear connecting paths have been shown for DNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR10 by several works.

Formally, let A:=\hat{f}(.,\theta_{A}) and B:=\hat{f}(.,\theta_{B}) two neural networks sharing a common architecture \hat{f}. They are parametrized by \theta_{A} and \theta_{B} after training those networks on a data distribution P with loss \mathcal{L}, i.e. by minimizing \mathcal{E}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P}[\mathcal{L}(\hat{f}(x,\theta),y)] over \theta. Let p be a continuous path connecting \theta_{A} and \theta_{B}, i.e. a continuous function defined on [0,1] with p(0)=\theta_{A} and p(1)=\theta_{B}. The problem of linear mode connectivity was first identified by earlier work, which defined the error barrier height of p as \sup_{t\in[0,1]}\mathcal{E}\left(p(t)\right)-\left((1-t)\mathcal{E}\left(\theta_{A}\right)+t\mathcal{E}\left(\theta_{B}\right)\right). The two solutions \theta_{A} and \theta_{B} are mode connected if there is a continuous path with zero error barrier height connecting them. If in addition p is linear, that is p(t)=(1-t)\theta_{A}+t\theta_{B},\, \theta_{A} and \theta_{B} are linearly mode connected (LMC).

Recently, two works pointed out that the units in a hidden layer of a model can be permuted and the network's functionality is preserved. Figure 1 shows how the hidden layer of a two-layer network can be permuted to match a different target network without changing the source function. From now on we understand LMC modulo permutation invariance, i.e. two networks A,B are linear mode connected when there is a permutation of neurons in each hidden layer of network B such that the linear path in parameter space between network A and permuted network B has low loss.

One of these works proposed to use optimal transport (OT) theory to find a soft alignment giving a “good match” (in a certain sense) between the neurons of two trained DNNs. The authors also propose ways to fuse the aligned networks together in a federated learning context with local-steps. The other work studied experimentally linear mode connectivity between two pre-aligned networks. They first align the weights of network B on the weights of network A and then connect both of them by a linear path in parameter space. They achieved zero-loss barrier for two Resnets trained with SGD on CIFAR10. Their experiments also strongly suggest that the error barrier on a linear path gets smaller for wider networks, and that big depth has a detrimental effect.

A recent work shows that dropout stable networks (i.e. networks that are functionally stable to the action of randomly setting a fraction of their weights and normalizing the others) exhibit mode connectivity. Another work uses a mean field viewpoint to show that wide two-layer neural networks trained with SGD are dropout stable, and so shows (non-linear) mode connectivity for two-layer neural networks in the mean field regime (i.e. one single wide hidden layer). Finally, another paper shows that two-layer neural networks exhibit linear mode connectivity up to permutation at initialization, for parameters initialized following uniform independent distribution properly scaled. They point out that this result could be extended to networks trained in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime, where parameters stay close to initialization.

The aim of this paper is to build theoretical foundations for the phenomenon of linear mode connectivity up to permutation. More precisely, we prove theoretically that this phenomenon arises naturally on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), which goes beyond the two-layer networks that theoretical works have focused on so far. We also give a new efficient way to find the right permutation to apply on the units of a layer of a neural network. The paper is organized as follows:

- In Section 3, we focus on two-layer neural networks in the mean field regime. Non-linear mode connectivity was already proved in this setting; we go further and prove linear mode connectivity up to permutation. We also give an upper bound on the minimal width of the hidden layer that guarantees linear mode connectivity.

- In Section 4, we use general OT theory to show tight asymptotics on the minimal width of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) that ensures LMC.

- In Section 5, we apply our general results to networks with parameters following sub-Gaussian distribution. Our result holds for deep networks, and generalizes the result of earlier work with better bounds. We explain the dependence in the dimension of the underlying distributions of the weights in each layer and how it connects with previous empirical observations. Using a model of approximately low dimensional weight distribution as a proxy of sparse feature learning, we get more realistic bounds on the architectures of DNNs that ensure linear mode connectivity. So we show why LMC is possible after training and how it depends on the complexity of the task. Finally we unify our framework with dropout stability.

- In Section 6, we validate the theoretical framework by showing how the implicit dimension of the weight distribution is correlated with linear mode connectivity for MLPs trained on MNIST with SGD, and we propose a new weight matching method.

Recently, [24,25] highlighted that the units in a hidden layer of a given model can be permuted while preserving the network’s functionality. Figure 1 shows how one can permute the hidden layer of a two-layer network to match a different target network without changing the source function. From now on, we understand LMC modulo permutation invariance, i.e. two networks A,B are said to be linear mode connected whenever there exists a permutation of neurons in each hidden layer of network B such that the linear path in parameter space between network A and the permuted network B has low loss.

[24] proposed to use optimal transport (OT) theory to find a soft alignment providing a “good match” (in a certain sense) between the neurons of two trained DNNs. The authors further propose ways to fuse the aligned networks together in a federated learning context with local-steps. [25] further studied experimentally the linear mode connectivity between two pre-aligned networks: they first align network B’s weights on those of network A before connecting both by a linear path in parameter space. They notably achieved a zero-loss barrier for two Resnets trained with SGD on CIFAR10. Moreover, their experiments strongly suggest that the error barrier on a linear path gets smaller for wider networks, while big depth has a detrimental effect.

A recent work by [26] shows that dropout stable networks (i.e. networks that are functionally stable to the action of randomly setting a fraction of their weights and normalizing the others) exhibit mode connectivity. [27] use a mean field viewpoint to show that wide two-layer neural networks trained with SGD are dropout stable, and hence show (non-linear) mode connectivity for two-layer neural networks in the mean field regime (i.e. one single wide hidden layer). Finally, [23] show that two-layer neural networks exhibit linear mode connectivity up to permutation at initialization for parameters initialized following a properly scaled uniform independent distribution. They highlight that this result could be extended to networks trained in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime, where parameters stay close to initialization [28].

This paper aims to build theoretical foundations for the phenomenon of linear mode connectivity up to permutation. More precisely, we prove theoretically that this phenomenon arises naturally on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), going beyond the two-layer networks on which theoretical works have focused so far. We also provide a new efficient way to find the right permutation to apply to the units of a neural network’s layer. The paper is organized as follows:

- • In Section 3, we focus on two-layer neural networks in the mean field regime. While [27] proved non-linear mode connectivity in this setting, we go further by proving linear mode connectivity up to permutation. Moreover, we provide an upper bound on the minimal width of the hidden layer that guarantees linear mode connectivity.

- • In Section 4, we use general OT theory to exhibit tight asymptotics on the minimal width of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to ensure LMC.

- • In Section 5, we apply our general results to networks with parameters following a sub-Gaussian distribution. Our result holds for deep networks and generalizes the result of [23] with better bounds. We shed light on the dependence on the dimension of the underlying distributions of the weights in each layer and explain how it connects with previous empirical observations [25]. Using a model of approximately low dimensional weight distribution as a proxy of sparse feature learning, we obtain more realistic bounds on the architectures of DNNs that ensure linear mode connectivity. We thereby show why LMC is possible after training and how it depends on the complexity of the task. Finally, we unify our framework with dropout stability.

- • In Section 6, we validate our theoretical framework by showing how the implicit dimension of the weight distribution correlates with linear mode connectivity for MLPs trained on MNIST with SGD, and we propose a new weight matching method.
